historical_timeline.summary: Beginning of a long illness described in his letter to a physician.
His mother had died by the time he went to live at his brother's house.
Struck with a disorder in his bowels.
Attending physician describes a hemorrhage in the upper intestines.
Wrote from Bath that his physicians disagreed about the diagnosis.
Described his illness as a diarrhoea of two years.
Died at Edinburgh; no examination after death.

claims.statement: David Hume was born at Edinburgh on April 26, 1711, Old Style (May 7, 1711, in the Gregorian calendar), the second son of Joseph Hume of Ninewells in Berwickshire.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The New Style date is the Old Style date plus eleven days; Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1752.

claims.statement: In My Own Life Hume wrote that his father died when he was an infant, leaving him, an elder brother, and a sister in their mother's care, and that his mother had died by the time he went to live at his brother's country house in 1749.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No cause of death is given for either parent in this source.

claims.statement: In a letter to a physician written about 1734, Hume described an illness beginning about September 1729, when he was eighteen: loss of his ardour for study, scurvy spots on his fingers, and from about April 1730 a watery mouth, which his physician called 'the disease of the learned'; he was treated with bitters, anti-hysteric pills, a pint of claret a day, and riding, and in 1731 had a ravenous appetite and palpitations.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary description and label only; no modern diagnosis is inferred.

claims.statement: In My Own Life, dated April 18, 1776, Hume wrote that in spring 1775 he was struck with a disorder in his bowels, which at first gave him no alarm but which he came to judge mortal and incurable; he wrote that he had suffered very little pain and that his spirits had never abated.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented onset that anchors the synthetic episode. His equanimity is recorded here as sourced history only.

claims.statement: In an undated letter written early in 1776, the physician attending Hume reported that he had been declining slowly for several years and more rapidly for about a year, with a sensation of excessive heat chiefly at night, and inferred a hemorrhage in the upper part of the intestines; the letter reports Hume's statement that his mother had the same constitution and died of the same disorder.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary physician's inference; the family history is Hume's own report as relayed in the letter.

claims.statement: Writing from Bath on May 13, 1776, Hume reported that his physicians disagreed about his disorder: one called it a hemorrhage, another a stricture ('spincture') of the colon that would be easy to cure, and a third a bilious complaint.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents that no agreed diagnosis was reached in his lifetime.

source_links.locator: Letter to Dr. Blair, Bath, 13th May 1776

claims.statement: Hume left Edinburgh in late April 1776, passing Morpeth on April 23, and travelled by London to Bath to take the waters; an early improvement had faded by June, and he returned to Edinburgh.

source_links.locator: Chapter 13, journal of the journey and letters of May and June 1776

claims.statement: In a letter of August 20, 1776, Hume described his distemper as a diarrhoea, or disorder in his bowels, which had been gradually undermining him for two years and had been visibly hastening his end within the last six months.

source_links.locator: Letter to the Comtesse de Boufflers, Edinburgh, 20th August 1776

claims.statement: Hume died at Edinburgh about four in the afternoon on August 25, 1776, aged 65; his physician wrote that he remained perfectly sensible and free from much pain to the last. His body was not opened after death, so the cause of his illness was never established.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

source_links.locator: Physician's letter of 26th August 1776 and the note on the burial

claims.statement: Hume's final illness has been interpreted retrospectively as colon cancer; a modern essay calls his death 'probably from colon cancer,' and a reference work describes a terminal abdominal cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation without pathology. Spread to the liver is sometimes suggested but was not confirmed in a fetched source and is not asserted.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize iron deficiency anemia with a change in bowel habit in a man of 64 as possible colorectal cancer; complete colonoscopy, staging CT, and CEA; coordinate preoperative intravenous iron, resection, and three months of adjuvant CAPOX; and begin survivorship surveillance on the CMID schedule with neuropathy and distress checks.

visit_schedule.purpose: Primary care visit for three months of looser stools with dark blood, tiredness, and weight loss
Review of colonoscopy, biopsy, and staging CT; intravenous iron; medical oncology consultation
Review four weeks after laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy, before adjuvant chemotherapy
Same-day sick visit for a head cold and cough during chemotherapy
Review two weeks after completing adjuvant CAPOX and start of survivorship surveillance

hpi.narrative: Mr. Hume returns three weeks after presenting with looser stools, dark blood, tiredness, and iron deficiency anemia. Colonoscopy thirteen days ago reached the cecum and found a 4 cm ulcerated mass at 28 cm in the sigmoid colon, which was biopsied and tattooed; there were no other lesions. The biopsy shows moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with intact mismatch-repair proteins. The staging CT eleven days ago showed two small pericolic lymph nodes, clear lungs, and one 9 mm indeterminate lesion in the liver. He still has two or three loose stools a day with dark blood on some days, and he tires on hills. His weight is down a further 0.8 kg. He saw Dr. Mehta of medical oncology this morning and has a colorectal surgery appointment this week. He took the news calmly and asked for the facts plainly; he wants to keep working on his books.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Hume returns two weeks after the last capecitabine dose of his fourth and final CAPOX cycle. The DPYD genotype before cycle 1 showed no decreased-function variant, and he received all four cycles on schedule at full dose. In cycle 2 he had three days of loose stools, controlled with loperamide. His September cold resolved without complications. Cold-triggered tingling after each oxaliplatin dose has left mild numbness of the fingertips and toe tips that does not interfere with buttoning, writing, or walking, and is not painful. He has no bowel bleeding or change in habit, no abdominal pain, cough, or bone pain. He walks 30 minutes a day and writes every morning. He feels well and asks what the follow-up will be.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Hume is a 64-year-old man with stage IIIB sigmoid colon cancer, resected in June, who is on day 9 of his third 21-day cycle of adjuvant CAPOX (oxaliplatin given on day 1, capecitabine on days 1 to 14). Three days ago he developed a runny nose and scratchy throat, followed by a dry cough. He called the oncology triage line this morning, as his chemotherapy plan instructs, and was asked to be seen in primary care today with a blood count. His home temperatures have been 37.1 to 37.4 °C, checked twice daily, and he has not taken acetaminophen, so no fever has been masked. A home COVID-19 antigen test yesterday was negative. He is eating and drinking normally, has had two soft stools a day without diarrhea, no mouth sores, and no redness or peeling of his palms or soles. The cold tingling in his fingers after each oxaliplatin dose settles within five days, as before. A friend who visited last week had a cold.

documentation.advance_care_planning: Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 20 minutes, with his consent, prompted by his cancer diagnosis. He has named a health care agent and completed a written health care directive, now scanned into the chart. If the cancer recurs, he wants a frank account of the options and their expected benefit, and he would accept surgery or chemotherapy that offered a real chance of cure or of more good time. He would not want resuscitation or prolonged life support if recovery to independent life and work were not expected, and he would want comfort-focused care at home at the end of life.

consultant_note.history: Mr. Hume is seen at the request of Dr. Gallacher three weeks after presenting with looser stools, dark rectal bleeding, tiredness, and iron deficiency anemia. Colonoscopy thirteen days ago found a 4 cm ulcerated, non-obstructing mass at 28 cm in the sigmoid colon and no other lesions; the biopsy shows moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. He still has two or three loose stools a day with some dark blood, and he tires on hills. He has no abdominal pain, obstructive symptoms, cough, or bone pain. He is independent, writes every morning, and wants plain information
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Colonoscopy report and biopsy pathology with mismatch-repair immunohistochemistry (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6 intact); CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis from eleven days ago; today's CEA 6.4 ng/mL, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, and normal liver tests; the presenting blood count and iron studies

exam.finding: Comfortable, pale
Conjunctival pallor
Soft, non-tender; no palpable mass; liver not enlarged; no ascites
No supraclavicular or inguinal nodes

assessment.assessment: Clinical stage T3 N1 on CT, mismatch-repair proficient, with a raised CEA. This is colon rather than rectal cancer and is not bulky or obstructing, so surgery first is standard; treatment before surgery is not needed. The final stage and the need for chemotherapy depend on the surgical pathology

Too small to characterize on CT. A single liver metastasis would change the plan to a combined approach, so it should be clarified before the operation; a benign lesion such as a hemangioma or cyst is more probable with normal liver tests
Hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL with absent iron stores. Correcting it before surgery lowers the chance of transfusion; with surgery about two weeks away, intravenous iron is the practical route

A mother reported to have died of a similar bowel disorder, of unknown nature and age, is uncertain information. The tumor is mismatch-repair proficient, which makes Lynch syndrome improbable, but current guidance supports offering germline testing to people with colorectal cancer

recommendations: MRI of the liver with contrast before surgery to characterize the 9 mm lesion
If the liver lesion is benign, proceed to laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy with lymph node dissection by the colorectal surgery team; no treatment before surgery
Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg now and again in one week, with a blood count and ferritin six to eight weeks later

After surgery: for low-risk stage III disease (T1 to T3 with one to three nodes), three months of CAPOX; for high-risk stage III disease, six months; for stage II disease without high-risk features, surveillance alone
Before any capecitabine, DPYD genotyping; check neuropathy at baseline and at every visit during and after oxaliplatin
Genetic counseling for germline testing after surgery
After treatment, surveillance by the CMID and NCCN schedule: CEA and examination every 3 to 6 months for two years, CT every 6 to 12 months for five years, and colonoscopy one year after resection
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Gallacher by telephone today and copied to the colorectal surgery team; the patient agrees with the plan and asked for the next steps in writing, which were given
consultant_note.follow_up: Medical oncology will see him two to three weeks after surgery with the pathology to decide on adjuvant therapy, and will give any chemotherapy. Primary care continues to coordinate iron treatment, mood and distress screening, and survivorship care
